title: Container image deployment works locally but fails in production
description: Diagnose why a .NET container runs with docker run locally but enters CrashLoopBackOff or ImagePullBackOff in Kubernetes, including image registries, security contexts, and probe misconfiguration.

data.text: The image runs on your laptop. The same tag is deployed to the production cluster and immediately crashes. The gap between local and production is almost always environmental: a missing environment variable, a security policy that blocks the container, a filesystem path that does not exist, or a registry authentication failure. Kubernetes gives you the clues—pod events, exit codes, and probe failures—but you have to know where to look.

data.title: Core concepts
items: Immutable image: a container image that is never modified after build
Image digest: a SHA256 hash that uniquely identifies an image, independent of mutable tags
Pod Security Standards: Kubernetes policies that control privilege escalation, hostPath mounts, and root execution
ConfigMap and Secret mounts: Kubernetes injects configuration as files or environment variables at runtime
Readiness and liveness probes: Kubernetes health checks that gate traffic and trigger restarts

terms.definition: A container image that is never modified after build. Any change requires a new image with a new tag or digest.
A SHA256 hash that uniquely identifies a container image, independent of mutable tags like latest.
Kubernetes settings that control privilege escalation, runAsUser, capabilities, and read-only root filesystems.
A Kubernetes pod state indicating the container is repeatedly crashing and the kubelet is backing off restart attempts.

items: Image built on Alpine but runs on a distroless base with different libc behavior
Hardcoded localhost or file paths that do not exist in the production container filesystem
Missing environment variables or secrets not injected by the production orchestrator
Port exposed in Dockerfile but not declared in Kubernetes containerPort
Pod security policy blocks privilege escalation or hostPath mounts required by the app
Image pulled from a private registry without proper secret or workload identity configured

cards.title: Reproduce in Staging
cards.description: Deploy the exact same image and Kubernetes manifests to a staging cluster that mirrors production.
cons: May not mirror production data or traffic patterns

cards.title: Ephemeral Debug Pod
cards.description: Run kubectl debug to inject a new container into the failing pod for interactive inspection.
pros: Fast access to pod filesystem and network
No need to change deployment manifests
Can install debugging tools on the fly
cons: May be blocked by security policies
Does not reproduce the exact startup sequence

cards.title: CI Pipeline Smoke Test
cards.description: Add integration tests that build the image, push it, and run a smoke test against a disposable cluster.
cons: Disposable clusters may not match production exactly

data.caption: Container deployment debugging flow from local build to production failure
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[docker build] --> B[Local Test]
    B -->|Pass| C[Push to Registry]
    C --> D[Kubernetes Deploy]
    D --> E{Image Pull?}
    E -->|No| F[Registry Auth Failure]
    E -->|Yes| G{Pod Start?}
    G -->|No| H[CrashLoopBackOff]
    G -->|Yes| I{Health Check Pass?}
    I -->|No| J[Readiness Probe Fail]
    I -->|Yes| K[Service Ready]

items: Inspect the failing pod events with kubectl describe pod and kubectl logs.
Compare the local Dockerfile base image with the production image digest.
Verify ConfigMap and Secret mounts match the application expectations.
Check Pod Security Standards or admission controllers for policy violations.
Run the container locally with the same environment variables and volumes as production.
Use kubectl debug to start an interactive shell in the failing pod namespace.

data.title: Avoid the latest tag
data.text: Never use the latest tag in production. It makes rollback impossible and debugging difficult because the image digest is unknown. Use immutable tags like git-SHA or semantic versions.

items: Build images once in CI and promote the same digest through all environments
Pin base images to a specific digest, not a floating tag
Run Trivy or Grype in CI to catch vulnerabilities before deployment
Include a startup probe with a generous initialDelaySeconds to handle slow initializations
Use Kubernetes secrets or CSI drivers instead of environment variables for sensitive data
Test deployments in a production-like cluster before the production window

items.question: Why does the pod say ImagePullBackOff?
items.answer: The cluster cannot pull the image. Check registry authentication, network egress rules, and whether the image tag or digest exists in the registry.

items.question: The container starts locally but crashes in Kubernetes. What should I check first?
items.answer: Check the exit code and logs. Common causes are missing environment variables, unreadable secrets, or file paths that differ between local and container environments.

data.title: Debug a failing Kubernetes deployment
data.description: A .NET API container runs fine with docker run locally but enters CrashLoopBackOff in production. Diagnose using kubectl events, logs, and a debug sidecar.
steps: Retrieve the pod events and identify the failure reason
Compare local environment variables with the Kubernetes ConfigMap
Check if the container user has permission to read mounted secrets
Use kubectl debug to inspect the filesystem and network inside the pod
Fix the manifest or Dockerfile and redeploy
data.expectedOutcome: You should identify a configuration or permission mismatch and implement a fix that prevents recurrence.

data.title: Summary
points: Treat containers as immutable: build once, run anywhere
Mirror production environment in staging for reliable testing
Use kubectl debug and events to diagnose pod failures quickly
Pin base images and avoid the latest tag
Automate security scanning and smoke tests in CI
data.takeaway: Local success is not a guarantee of production success. Design your container pipeline to catch environment-specific failures before they reach users.
